---
title: "Exercise: hierarchical segmentation and merge trees"
---

## Goal

By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

- build a **merge tree** by altitude, dynamics and area, and read partitions from it,
- compute an **ultrametric contour map** and threshold it,
- run **greedy merging** on a region adjacency graph,
- predict which hierarchy keeps which structure,
- *(math)* prove the ultrametric inequality and the link between the dynamics hierarchy and h-minima.

## Background

| Idea | What it means |
|---|---|
| Merge tree | leaves = initial regions; each merge makes a parent node at a level; levels never decrease going up |
| Cut at level $t$ | apply every merge with level $\le t$; regions = subtrees below the cut |
| Altitude hierarchy | merge basins across passes in increasing order (= single linkage on pass heights) |
| Attribute hierarchy | flood by altitude; at each meeting, the merge gets the attribute of the **smaller** region (dynamics = pass − its minimum; area; volume = area × depth); then sort the merges by these values |
| Ultrametric | $u(p, q)$ = level at which $p$ and $q$ first share a region |
| UCM | each boundary gets the $u$ of the regions on its two sides; thresholding gives the partitions |
| RAG merging | always merge the most similar adjacent pair (e.g. smallest difference of means), update, repeat |

## By hand

**B1.** A 1D landscape with five basins a–e (left to right): minima $1, 3, 0, 4, 2$; passes a|b 5, b|c 4, c|d 7, d|e 6; widths (areas) $10, 2, 8, 3, 6$.
(a) Build the merge tree by **altitude**. Which three regions remain after two merges?
(b) Compute the dynamics of each basin (c is the global minimum) and build the tree by **dynamics**. Three regions?
(c) Build the tree by **area** (when two regions meet at a pass, the smaller area dies; the merged region's area is the sum). Three regions?
(d) Build it by **volume** = area × (pass − minimum) of the smaller region.

**B2.** The UCM of the dynamics hierarchy of B1 assigns a value to each of the four boundaries a|b, b|c, c|d, d|e. (a) Write the four values. (b) Threshold at 3: which boundaries remain, and which regions? (c) Which threshold gives the h-minima watershed with $h = 4.5$?

**B3.** A $3 \times 3$ grid of regions with mean grey levels (4-neighbours)
$$\begin{bmatrix} 10 & 12 & 30 \\ 11 & 25 & 31 \\ 40 & 26 & 50 \end{bmatrix}.$$
Run greedy merging by difference of means. Give each merge with its difference until one region is left. What are the three regions just before the last two merges?

**B4.** **Predict.** A small bright spot (area 20 pixels, depth 80) and a large faint blob (area 2000, depth 5) sit on a flat background. Which of the hierarchies altitude, dynamics, area and volume keeps the spot longest? Which keeps the blob longest?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions"}
**B1.** (a) Passes in increasing order: b|c 4, a|b 5, d|e 6, c|d 7. Tree: (b, c) at 4; a joins at 5; (d, e) at 6; all at 7. After two merges: $\{a, b, c\}, \{d\}, \{e\}$.
(b) Dynamics = how far you climb before reaching a deeper basin: b (min 3) via b|c 4 to c: 1. d (4) via d|e 6 to e (2): 2. a (1) via a|b 5 to c (0): 4. e (2) via d|e 6, c|d 7 to c: 5. Flooding by altitude: b|c at 4 (b dies, value 1), a|b at 5 (a dies: $5 - 1 = 4$ vs $5 - 0 = 5$), d|e at 6 (d dies: 2), c|d at 7 ({d, e} dies: $7 - 2 = 5$). Sorted: b|c 1, d|e 2, a|b 4, c|d 5. Three regions: $\{a\}, \{b, c\}, \{d, e\}$.
(c) b|c at 4: areas 2 and 8: value 2 ({b, c} has 10). a|b at 5: {a} 10 and {b, c} 10: value 10. d|e at 6: 3 and 6: value 3 ({d, e} has 9). c|d at 7: {a, b, c} 20 and {d, e} 9: value 9. Sorted: b|c 2, d|e 3, c|d 9, a|b 10: b into c, d into e, {d, e} into {b, c}, then a. Three regions: $\{a\}, \{b, c\}, \{d, e\}$.
(d) b|c: $2 \cdot (4 - 3) = 2$ vs $8 \cdot 4 = 32$: 2. a|b: $10 \cdot 4 = 40$ vs $10 \cdot 5 = 50$: 40. d|e: $3 \cdot 2 = 6$ vs $6 \cdot 4 = 24$: 6. c|d: $20 \cdot 7 = 140$ vs $9 \cdot 5 = 45$: 45. Sorted: 2, 6, 40, 45: b|c, d|e, a|b, c|d: the same order as dynamics here.

**B2.** (a) a|b 4, b|c 1, c|d 5, d|e 2. (b) Boundaries with value > 3 remain: a|b and c|d. Regions $\{a\}, \{b, c\}, \{d, e\}$. (c) The h-minima with $h = 4.5$ keep the minima with dynamics ≥ 4.5: c (global) and e (5): two regions, $\{a, b, c\}$ and $\{d, e\}$. Threshold the UCM at 4.5: only c|d (5) remains. Same partition.

**B3.** Step 1: three pairs with difference 1: 10–11, 30–31, 25–26 (ties; any order). Step 2: {10, 11} (mean 10.5) and 12: 1.5. Step 3: {25, 26} (25.5) and {30, 31} (30.5): 5. Step 4: 40 joins {25, 26, 30, 31} (mean 28): 12 (its other neighbour, {10, 11, 12} with mean 11, differs by 29). Step 5: {10, 11, 12} (11) and {25, 26, 30, 31, 40} (30.4): 19.4. Step 6: 50 joins the rest (mean 23.1): 26.9. Before the last two merges: $\{10, 11, 12\}$, $\{25, 26, 30, 31, 40\}$, $\{50\}$.

**B4.** The spot: deep but tiny. Altitude: its pass is high (bright spot on flat background): kept long. Dynamics 80: kept long. Area 20: dies early. Volume $20 \cdot 80 = 1600$, compared with the blob's $2000 \cdot 5 = 10\,000$: dies before the blob. So dynamics (and altitude) keep the spot longest. The blob: area and volume keep it longest; dynamics (5) and altitude (low pass) remove it early.
:::

### Math questions

**B5.** *(math)* Prove the ultrametric inequality $u(p, r) \le \max(u(p, q), u(q, r))$ for any merge tree. Show that it implies: of the three distances among any three points, the two largest are equal.

**B6.** *(math)* Show that cutting the dynamics hierarchy at level $h$ gives the same partition as the watershed from the h-minima (minima with dynamics $\ge h$ as markers), assuming all dynamics differ from $h$.

**B7.** *(math)* Show that for the single-linkage (altitude) tree, $u(p, q)$ equals the minimax distance between $p$ and $q$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions (math)"}
**B5.** At level $t = \max(u(p,q), u(q,r))$ the region containing $q$ contains both $p$ and $r$ (nesting: once together, always together; regions of a partition are disjoint). So $u(p, r) \le t$. For three points, suppose $u(p, r)$ is strictly the largest; then $u(p, r) > \max(u(p,q), u(q,r))$, contradicting the inequality. So the largest value occurs at least twice.

**B6.** In the altitude flooding, a basin "dies" when it first meets a basin with a deeper minimum; its dynamics is the pass height minus its minimum, which is its extinction value in the dynamics hierarchy. Cutting at $h$ applies exactly the merges of basins whose dynamics is below $h$: each such basin is merged into the region of the deeper basin it meets. The minima with dynamics ≥ h survive, one region each. That is the h-minima watershed: the h-minima transform fills every basin shallower than $h$ up to its lowest pass, which joins it to a deeper neighbour, and flooding from the remaining minima assigns each pixel accordingly. (Boundary positions on the filled plateaus can differ by tie rules; the regions correspond one to one.)

**B7.** Merges happen in increasing order of edge weight; $p$ and $q$ first share a region at the weight $t$ of the edge whose union joined their components. Before that, all edges $< t$ did not connect them, so every path between them has an edge $\ge t$: minimax distance $\ge t$. After it, they are connected using edges $\le t$ only: minimax distance $\le t$. Hence $u(p, q)$ = minimax distance.
:::

## Explore: merge trees {#explore}

Initial regions (leaves) are watershed basins of the gradient, FH regions or SLIC superpixels of a synthetic image of touching **nuclei**, a **test scene**, an image with a **weak spot**, or the micrograph. Choose a hierarchy; the left panel shows the partition at the current cut (mean grey levels, yellow boundaries), the middle one the UCM, the bottom the dendrogram (y = merge order; drag to move the cut). For the synthetic images, the readout counts the true objects matched with IoU ≥ 0.5. Click a region to select its branch; **merge up** and **split** change the cut on that branch only.

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../demos/dist/demo.css">
<div data-demo="mergetree" data-preset="altitude"></div>
<script src="../demos/dist/mergetree.js"></script>
```

**M1.** Preset **altitude** (20 regions). How many of the 18 nuclei are matched? Move the cut: what is the best number you can reach, and at how many regions?

**M2.** Presets **dynamics vs altitude** and **area** at 20 regions: how many nuclei are matched? Which nuclei does the altitude hierarchy lose, and why?

**M3.** Choose **RAG: mean diff.** on the nuclei. How many are matched at 20 regions? Why is this criterion worse here, although it was better on the weak-spot image?

**M4.** Presets **cheapest edge leaks…** and **… mean difference does not** (2 regions). What does each keep? Set 3 regions in both.

**M5.** Preset **per-branch cut**: find a pair of touching nuclei that is one region, click it and press **split**. Then find a nucleus in two pieces and press **merge up** on one piece. Does the matched count go up?

**M6.** Preset **UCM thresholds** (micrograph): which boundaries are brightest in the UCM? Change the leaves to **SLIC**: how does the UCM change?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions"}
**M1.** 13 of 18 at 20 regions; the best is 13 (at 16 regions). The altitude hierarchy merges each nucleus with the background as soon as its weakest boundary point is reached; dim nuclei and touching pairs go early.

**M2.** Dynamics: 14 of 18; area: 16 of 18 (volume also 16). Their best values are 16 (dynamics, at 22 regions) and 17 (area, at 21). The altitude hierarchy loses dim nuclei (low passes to the background) and keeps fragments of large bright nuclei separate too long; area merges small fragments first, which is what an over-segmented nucleus needs.

**M3.** 10 of 18 at 20 regions (12 at best, at 45 regions). The nuclei have internal texture and touch each other with similar means: the mean difference between two halves of one nucleus is not smaller than that between two touching nuclei, and the background (one huge region) absorbs dim nuclei whose means are close to it. Mean difference helps against a single weak pixel, not against similar neighbours.

**M4.** Altitude: the dark disc stays, the bright disc has leaked into the background through its weak spot. Mean difference: the bright disc (with the ramp wedge) stays, the dark disc has merged. At 3 regions both hierarchies keep both discs (2 of 2 matched).

**M5.** Yes: splitting a merged pair and merging a fragmented nucleus each add a matched nucleus; a per-branch cut can beat every horizontal cut, because different nuclei need different levels.

**M6.** The nuclear envelope and the large dark structures of the cytoplasm are the brightest (most lasting) boundaries; small texture boundaries are dark. With SLIC leaves the UCM also contains the regular superpixel boundaries, most of which disappear early (dark), and the big boundaries are smoother.
:::

## Where this leads

The quality of a hierarchy depends on its leaves. [Superpixels](../superpixels/lec.qmd) are leaves designed for this: compact, about equal in size, and respecting the boundaries.
